text: A trademark is a distinctive sign, symbol, word, phrase, logo, or combination thereof that identifies and distinguishes the goods or services of one enterprise from those of others. Under the Trade Marks Act 1999, trademarks serve three main functions: origin function (indicating the source of goods/services), quality function (representing consistent quality), and advertising function (promoting the brand). For AYUSH products, trademarks can protect brand names like 'Chyawanprash Supreme', logos featuring traditional symbols, and taglines like 'Ancient Wisdom, Modern Science'. Unlike patents (20 years), trademarks can be renewed indefinitely every 10 years as long as they remain in use.

Trademark registration in India involves: 1) Trademark search on the IP India website to check availability and avoid conflicts with existing marks. 2) Filing application (Form TM-A) with the Trademarks Registry — can be filed online via ipindia.gov.in or physically at Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, or Ahmedabad offices. 3) Examination by the Registry (typically 12-18 months) — examiner checks for distinctiveness, similarity to existing marks, and prohibited categories. 4) Publication in the Trade Marks Journal for 4 months — allows third parties to file oppositions. 5) If no opposition or opposition resolved, registration certificate issued. 6) Total timeline: 18-24 months typically. E-filing reduces fees by 10%.

AYUSH products typically fall under these Nice Classification classes: Class 3 (cosmetics, toiletries, essential oils, perfumes — for Ayurvedic cosmetics and beauty products), Class 5 (pharmaceuticals, medicinal preparations, dietary supplements — for Ayurvedic medicines and health supplements), Class 29 (processed foods, oils, fats — for Ayurvedic food products), Class 30 (teas, spices, condiments — for herbal teas and formulations), Class 35 (retail services, advertising — for Ayurvedic clinics and wellness centers), Class 42 (scientific research services — for AYUSH R&D), Class 44 (medical services, healthcare — for Ayurvedic treatment centers). Multiple class filing is allowed but fees apply per class.

Trademark registration fees in India (2024): Filing fee for individuals/startups/small enterprises: Rs 4,500 (e-filing) or Rs 5,000 (physical). Filing fee for others (companies): Rs 9,000 (e-filing) or Rs 10,000 (physical). Per-class fee applies — each additional class costs the same as the first. Renewal fee (every 10 years): Rs 9,000 (e-filing) or Rs 10,000 (physical). Late renewal surcharge: Rs 3,000 (within 6 months of expiry) or Rs 5,000 (6-12 months). Expedited examination request: additional Rs 20,000. Opposition filing: Rs 2,700. Hearing fee: varies by case complexity.

Trade name (also called trading name or business name) is the name under which a business operates, registered under the Companies Act or Partnership Act. Trademark is a brand identifier registered under the Trade Marks Act 1999 to protect IP. Key differences: Trade names protect the business entity name (e.g., 'Dabur India Ltd'), while trademarks protect product brands (e.g., 'Dabur Chyawanprash', 'Dabur Honey'). A company can have one trade name but multiple trademarks. Trade name registration doesn't prevent others from using similar names for products; trademark does. For AYUSH businesses, register BOTH: trade name for legal entity, trademarks for each product line.

Trademark infringement occurs when an unauthorized party uses a mark identical or deceptively similar to a registered trademark in connection with goods/services for which it is registered. Section 29 of Trade Marks Act 1999 defines infringement. Remedies include: injunction (court order to stop use), damages (monetary compensation), account of profits (surrender of infringer's profits), delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. For AYUSH sector, common infringement includes: counterfeit Ayurvedic medicines using famous brand names, similar packaging trade dress, and misleading online listings. Criminal prosecution possible under Section 103-104 with imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 2 lakh.

Collective marks are trademarks owned by an association whose members use them to identify themselves with a level of quality or geographical origin. Example: 'Kashmiri Saffron' used by Kashmir saffron growers' association. Certification marks indicate that goods/services meet defined standards set by a certifying organization. Example: ISI mark, AGMARK, FSSAI logo. For AYUSH: The AYUSH Premium Mark is a certification mark for quality-certified Ayurvedic/AYUSH products. GI (Geographical Indication) overlaps with collective marks for location-specific products like 'Darjeeling Tea' or 'Nashik Grapes'. Collective marks cost Rs 9,000 (e-filing); certification marks require demonstrating the certification standards.

Well-known trademarks receive enhanced protection beyond their registered class under Section 11(6)-(10) of Trade Marks Act 1999. A trademark becomes well-known through extensive use, advertising, consumer recognition, and reputation. Well-known marks are protected against: use in unrelated goods/services, dilution of distinctiveness, and tarnishment of reputation. Examples: 'Tata', 'Reliance', 'Bajaj', 'Himalaya' (for wellness products). For AYUSH brands, achieving well-known status requires: decades of use, pan-India presence, significant advertising spend, consumer surveys showing recognition, and awards/accolades. The Registrar maintains a list of well-known marks; brands can apply for inclusion.

To protect trademarks internationally, options include: 1) Madrid Protocol (India joined 2013) — single application through WIPO covers 130+ member countries, centralized renewal, cost-effective for multi-country filing. 2) Paris Convention priority — file in other countries within 6 months of Indian filing to claim priority date. 3) Direct national filing — file separately in each country's trademark office. For AYUSH exporters, Madrid Protocol is recommended: file Indian application first, then designate countries like USA, EU, UAE, Japan via Madrid. Fees: base fee ~653 Swiss francs + per-country designation fees (varying from 73 to 100+ Swiss francs per class per country). Timeline: 12-18 months per country for examination.

A registered trademark must be used within 5 years of registration, otherwise it becomes vulnerable to cancellation for non-use under Section 47. 'Use' means affixing the mark to goods, using on packaging, displaying in advertisements, and using in trade invoices. For AYUSH businesses, maintain evidence of use: sales invoices, product photos, advertising materials, export documents. Defensive registrations (marks registered but not intended for use, only to block others) are risky and can be removed. If not using a mark for legitimate reasons (regulatory delays, production issues), document the reasons — 'special circumstances' can excuse non-use.

Comprehensive brand protection for AYUSH businesses: 1) Trademark for brand names and logos (product identity), 2) Patent for novel formulations and processes (technical innovation), 3) Trade secret for traditional family recipes (confidential know-how), 4) Copyright for marketing materials, packaging artwork (creative expression), 5) Design registration for unique bottle/packaging shapes (visual appearance), 6) Domain name registration for .in, .com, and relevant TLDs (online presence), 7) GI registration if product is location-specific (geographical identity). Portfolio approach: combine multiple IP rights for maximum protection. Budget allocation: trademarks first (most cost-effective), then patents for genuinely novel innovations.

Any person can file opposition within 4 months of trademark publication in Trade Marks Journal. Opposition grounds include: similarity to earlier mark, lack of distinctiveness, descriptive/generic term, mark obtained by fraud, mark contrary to law/morality. Process: 1) Notice of opposition (Form TM-O) filed by opponent with fees Rs 2,700. 2) Counter-statement by applicant within 2 months. 3) Evidence stage — both parties submit affidavits. 4) Hearing before Registrar. 5) Decision — typically takes 2-3 years. For AYUSH marks, common opposition bases: similarity to established Ayurvedic brands, use of common Ayurvedic ingredient names (which may be descriptive). Defense: prove acquired distinctiveness through use.
